solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Portraits in water-colours? Could be the Ugly Sisters, no doubt!

definitions.meaning: pictures done in water-colour paint are literally not done in oils

definitions.text: Could be the Ugly Sisters, no doubt!
definitions.meaning: the idiom for a plain-looking person, fitting Cinderella's pantomime stepsisters

explanation.surface: A musing on what kind of picture you might paint of Cinderella's unlovely stepsisters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ugly Sisters are Cinderella's stepsisters, comic villains of the British Christmas pantomime.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, watercolours use no oils; idiomatically, saying someone is not much to look at uses the same phrase.

clue.text: Command in army rifle drill. — or a clue for Mars?

parts.note: the phrase read as an instruction says rearrange the letters of the weapons word, which turns them into the planet's name

explanation.surface: A parade-ground order, then a playful aside suggesting a clue for the god of war.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as wordplay, the phrase tells you to put ARMS in a different order, giving MARS.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the drill word of command telling soldiers to bring their rifles to rest beside the right foot.

clue.text: Apart from starter, cooking hailed as perfect

indicators.note: cooking is fiddling or doctoring, so the remaining letters are rearranged
the first letter of the following word is dropped, starter meaning its opening

explanation.surface: A dish, apart from its first course, is acclaimed as flawless cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apart from starter' drops the H of HAILED, leaving AILED; 'cooking' rearranges those letters. The kitchen words make 'starter' look like a first course.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something that could not be bettered, so they are synonyms as adjectives.

clue.text: Percentiles Ted worked out for one (almost) in White House

indicators.note: worked out suggests letters being processed and solved into a new order

explanation.surface: Statistics about a man named Ted being calculated, apparently for a Washington resident.
explanation.walkthrough: Someone chosen at the November election but not yet sworn in is 'almost' in the White House.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has won the US election but not yet been inaugurated is nearly the occupant of the executive residence.

clue.text: Attempt to infuse alloy of tin to make gold, possibly

indicators.note: to infuse is to pour into, so one piece goes inside the other
an alloy is a mixture of metals, so the letters following are mixed up

parts.note: an attempt is a go, as in 'have a go'

explanation.surface: An alchemist's attempt to turn a tin mixture into gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alloy of' gives INT, and 'to infuse' does the containing; the alchemy surface hides that 'gold' is only an example of the metal cast this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast bar of metal is often gold, so gold is given as an example of what such a bar may be.

clue.text: Little bird the French catch when climbing — 13 role for 29

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
le is French for the

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means the word reads upwards, so backwards

parts.note: to catch is to trap

explanation.surface: A small bird and a French article caught on the way up, then a theatrical aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is THE BEST and 29 is CHARACTER ACTOR: the best role for a character actor is the one the play is named after.
explanation.definitionFit: The role named in a play's heading is usually the lead, the plum part an actor craves.

clue.text: Snare none of our soldiers expected, initially

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of each of the five words before it

explanation.surface: A trap that none of our troops anticipated.
explanation.definitionFit: A running loop of rope that tightens is a classic trap, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Seem dead trendy, oddly, though drugged

indicators.note: oddly picks the letters in odd positions of the three words

explanation.surface: Someone appears deathly fashionable but is in fact under the influence.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone given a calming drug is in a sedative state, so the past participles are synonyms.

clue.text: Where country folk may work and play

definitions.text: Where country folk may work and play

parts.words: Where country folk may work and play
parts.note: a small village where rural people live and work, and also the title of Shakespeare's Danish tragedy

explanation.walkthrough: 'play' seems to mean leisure, but it is a stage play: the word is both a little village and Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny rural settlement is a place where villagers labour, and the same word names a famous drama.

clue.text: Walk like a duck (headless!), so become confused

indicators.note: headless means the first letter is taken off

parts.note: to waddle is to walk with a duck's rolling gait

explanation.surface: A duck without its head waddles about in bewilderment.
explanation.definitionFit: To muddle or grow muddled; the verb also means to become confused, as an egg goes bad.

clue.text: Transport of delight may be so much more

indicators.note: to transport is to carry from place to place, so these letters are moved around

explanation.surface: A rapture of joy might be multiplied many times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport of delight' reads as a phrase meaning ecstasy; 'Transport' is the anagram signal working on 'of delight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Multiplied by eight is a great deal more, so the clue's vague 'so much more' is a playful definition.

clue.text: Old sayings lie about an entrancing maiden

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge and sayings handed down

indicators.note: about means the letters are turned around and rearranged

explanation.surface: Ancient proverbs tell untruths about a bewitching girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges LIE into LEI. The Rhine siren whose singing lured boatmen onto the rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: In German legend she is a beautiful siren on the Rhine whose song enchants sailors to their doom.

clue.text: First-class punishment once given in sixes, apparently

definitions.text: punishment once given in sixes, apparently
definitions.meaning: school caning came as 'six of ...', six strokes at a time

explanation.surface: A top-grade punishment that used to be handed out six at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six of the best' was a British school caning of six strokes, so the phrase seems to come in sixes.
explanation.definitionFit: Finest quality fits the first sense, and the old caning phrase supplies the second humorously.

clue.text: Bother about losing English pound

indicators.note: about signals the letters being turned around into a new order
losing says a letter is shed from the scrambled pool

explanation.surface: Worry over losing an English pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges BOTHER, and 'losing' takes E away from the pool. 'pound' looks like money but is the verb or noun of beating.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart may pound or beat heavily; the two words are synonyms for a strong rhythmic pulse.

clue.text: Did she succeed where Canute failed?

definitions.text: Did she succeed where Canute failed?

parts.words: Did she succeed where Canute failed?
parts.note: King Canute famously could not command the tide, while the song says the British personification 'rules the waves'

explanation.walkthrough: Canute was the English king who set his throne by the sea and failed to stop the tide; the patriotic song 'Rule, Britannia!' says she rules the waves.
explanation.definitionFit: The female emblem of Britain is hailed in song as ruler of the waves, mastering the sea Canute could not.

clue.text: Accounted for wife once getting basic education

parts.note: a former wife is an ex
basic means plain, unadorned

explanation.surface: A former wife finally getting some elementary schooling is the explanation.
explanation.definitionFit: To account for something is to give the reasons for it, so the past forms are synonyms.

clue.text: He buys nearly neat vodka after a beer

indicators.note: nearly means the last letter is left off

parts.note: neat spirit is pure, undiluted
a chaser is a spirit drunk after a beer

explanation.surface: A man ordering almost undiluted vodka after his pint.
explanation.definitionFit: A buyer is one who makes a purchase, so the noun phrase 'he buys' describes him.

clue.text: The big cheese à l'italienne

parts.note: the most important person, put in Italian words meaning 'number one'

explanation.walkthrough: 'big cheese' tempts towards an Italian cheese such as parmesan; it is slang for the boss.
explanation.definitionFit: The top person is number one, and the Italian phrase for that is used in English slang.

clue.text: Anaesthetic more convenient for a heating engineer

parts.note: gas, such as nitrous oxide, is used as an anaesthetic
fitter means more suitable or convenient

explanation.surface: A patient wondering if gas is the better anaesthetic, with a nod to a boiler mechanic.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesperson who installs and services gas appliances such as boilers is a heating engineer.

clue.text: Boy or girl given endless credit that's inherited

parts.note: Gene is a name used for both men and women

indicators.note: endless means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: tick is informal British for credit, as in buying on tick

explanation.surface: A child granted unlimited credit, a trait passed down in the family.
explanation.walkthrough: Buying 'on tick' is British slang for buying on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Traits passed down from parents are carried in the genes, so 'inherited' fits.

clue.text: Not so Wild West Americans admit to

indicators.note: admit means let in, so the words hold the answer inside them

explanation.surface: Westerners in the US confess that the Wild West was less wild than claimed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild West' reads as one phrase, but 'Wild' ends the definition and 'West' starts the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative adjective: less wild means more docile and domesticated.

clue.text: Part of breakfast less carefully prepared?

definitions.meaning: a slice of bacon, part of a cooked breakfast
more reckless, the comparative of hasty or impetuous

explanation.surface: A breakfast item, apparently cooked with less care.
explanation.definitionFit: A slice of bacon on the plate, and the comparative of an adjective meaning hasty and careless.

clue.text: Recount managed the wrong way by judge

indicators.note: the wrong way means the word reads backwards

parts.note: ran means managed, as a business
to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: A judge ran the recount the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' turns RAN into NAR. 'Recount' looks like a vote count; it means tell.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount a story is to tell it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Former capital needs Germany's agreement for Spanish export

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro was Brazil's capital until 1960
ja is German for yes

explanation.surface: A former capital city needs German approval to send goods to Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A red wine from northern Spain shipped widely abroad, so it is an example of an export.

clue.text: See 4
The part of the skeleton's said to be amusing

indicators.note: said to be means the word sounds like another when spoken

parts.note: amusing means funny or comic

explanation.surface: A bone joke: the funny bone part of the skeleton is called amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'funny bone' is at the elbow end of this upper-arm bone, which explains the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the long bone of the upper arm, a component of the human skeleton.

clue.text: Kind of bullet (40% silver) that doesn't kill — it cures!

definitions.text: Kind of bullet (40% silver) that doesn't kill — it cures!

parts.words: Kind of bullet (40% silver) that doesn't kill — it cures!
parts.note: a 'bullet' that is a miracle cure; two of its five letters spell the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.walkthrough: A silver bullet kills werewolves; this bullet heals. AG, the symbol for silver, makes up two of the five letters, hence 40%.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug or remedy that cures a disease completely is called a miracle bullet with this adjective.

clue.text: Heart of sweetcorn, lacking keratin, is non-prickly

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

parts.note: horn is made of keratin, so lacking it means hornless

explanation.surface: Sweetcorn with its core lacking a protein is not prickly.
explanation.walkthrough: Keratin is the protein of which horn is made.
explanation.definitionFit: A rose stem without spines is not prickly, so the adjectives match.

clue.text: Basic food brought back to protect gold standard

indicators.note: to protect is to surround, so one piece encloses the other
brought back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: an egg is a staple food
AU is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Staple food returned to guard the gold standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' turns EGG into GGE, and 'to protect' wraps it round AU. 'gold standard' reads as one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A measure or criterion for judging things, as in a test or yardstick, is a synonym of standard.

clue.text: Card-player, devotee of the Method, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a card is an eccentric person, a character, and a player is an actor
a Method actor immerses in a role; one who plays distinctive supporting types might

explanation.surface: Someone at the card table, or a follower of Stanislavski's acting system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card-player' seems to be a bridge or poker player; 'card' means an eccentric and 'player' a performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who specialises in quirky, distinctive roles; such a performer may use the Method style of acting.
